title: Comprehensive Chronological and Epigraphical Genealogy of Ancient India: From Cosmic Genesis and Epic Kings to Historical Dynasties
subtitle: Synchronization of Puranic King-Lists (Pargiter AIHT), Epigraphical Charters (Pallava, Chola, Pandya, Andhra Ikshvaku), and Tamil Sangam Traditions
compiler_credentials: Archival Historian, Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute & Asiatic Society Fellowships
abstract: An exhaustive scholarly reconstruction bridging Puranic-Epic genealogies (Manu, Ikshvaku, Rama, Pururavas, Bharata, Parikshit, Brihadbala) to epigraphically verified historical dynasties (Brihadrathas, Pradyotas, Haryankas, Nandas, Mauryas, Andhra Ikshvaku, Cholas, Pandyas, Cheras, Pallavas). Synthesizes F.E. Pargiter's 'Ancient Indian Historical Tradition' (AIHT), BORI Critical Editions, Epigraphia Indica, South Indian Inscriptions, and Tamil Sangam literature into a singular ontological answer to 'Who We Are? / யார் நாம்?'.

foundational_frameworks.work: Ancient Indian Historical Tradition (AIHT, Oxford University Press, 1922) and The Purana Text of the Dynasties of the Kali Age (1913)
methodological_principles: Distinction between Kshatriya bardic tradition (Sutas, Magadhas) and Brahmanical priestly traditions, demonstrating that dynastic genealogies in Vayu, Matsya, Brahmanda, and Vishnu Puranas were derived from metrical royal chronicles preserved in Prakrit and later Sanskritized.
Synchronization of contemporary dynastic lines across Aryavarta using inter-dynastic marriages, wars, and teacher-pupil (Guru-Shishya) lineages as horizontal anchors.
Establishment of a 95-generation index from Vaivasvata Manu (Gen 1) to the Bharata War (Gen 95), placing Sri Rama at Gen 65, Mandhatri at Gen 21, and Sagara at Gen 41.
Reconstruction of Kali Age dynasties using the prophetic future-tense ('Bhavishya') sections of the Matsya, Vayu, and Brahmanda Puranas, synchronized with Jain and Buddhist canonical records.

contributions: Critical Edition of the Mahabharata (1919-1966, under V.S. Sukthankar, S.K. Belvalkar, P.L. Vaidya), collating 1,259 manuscripts in diverse scripts (Sarada, Malayalam, Grantha, Devanagari, Bengali, Telugu, Newari) to establish the archetype recension of the Bharata genealogy.
Systematic critical analysis of Puranic genealogies confirming the pan-Indian geographic dispersion of Lunar and Solar clans after the Bharata war.

Initial identification of 'Sandrocottus' with Chandragupta Maurya (Sir William Jones, 1793), establishing the principal chronological synchronism ('sheet-anchor') connecting Indian and Greco-Roman records.
Decipherment of Brahmi and Kharosthi scripts by James Prinsep (1837-1838), unlocking Ashoka's rock edicts and pillar inscriptions.
Publication of epigraphical compendia and critical translations of the Vishnu Purana (H.H. Wilson, 1840) and Indian Epigraphy / Epigraphical Glossary (D.C. Sircar).

sources: South Indian Inscriptions (SII, Volumes I-XXXVII), Archaeological Survey of India.
Epigraphia Indica (EI, Volumes I-XLII), notably Anbil Plates (EI XV), Kanyakumari Inscription (EI XVIII), Velvikkudi Grant (EI XVII), Nagarjunakonda Inscriptions (EI XX, XXI).
Sangam Classics: Purananuru, Patirruppattu, Ahananuru, Silappadikaram, Manimekalai, and commentators Nachinarkkiniyar, Ilampuranar, and Adiyarkkunallar.

cosmic_and_primordial_lineage.primordial_roots: Parabrahman / Narayana -> Brahma -> Manasa Putras (Saptarishis and Prajapatis)

solar_root_suryavamsa.origin: Brahma -> Marichi -> Kashyapa (married Aditi) -> Vivasvan (Surya) -> Sraddhadeva (Vaivasvata Manu)
solar_root_suryavamsa.significance: Founder of the premier Solar dynasty of Ayodhya and universal ethical kingship.

lunar_root_chandravamsa.origin: Brahma -> Atri -> Chandra (Soma) -> Budha (married Ila, daughter of Manu) -> Pururavas Aila
lunar_root_chandravamsa.significance: Founder of the Aila / Lunar race encompassing Pauravas, Kurus, Yadavas, Pandavas, and Tamil Pandyas.

rishi_brahma_kshatra_root.origin: Brahma -> Angiras -> Brihaspati -> Samyu -> Bharadvaja -> Drona -> Ashvatthama -> Pallava
rishi_brahma_kshatra_root.significance: The sacred fusion of spiritual asceticism (Brahma) and sovereign martial rule (Kshatra) embodied in the Pallavas of Kanchi.

pargiter_genealogical_synchronization_ta.description: Chronological alignment of major pre-Bharata dynastic generations based on F.E. Pargiter's AIHT (Generations 1 to 95)

synchronisms.notes: Vaivasvata Manu distributes the Earth among his sons: Ikshvaku receives Madhyadesha (Ayodhya), Ila's son Pururavas rules Pratishthana (Prayaga).

synchronisms.lunar_aila: Yayati (Gen 4/5: divides empire between Yadu, Turvasu, Druhyu, Anu, Puru)
synchronisms.notes: Kakutstha defeats Asuras standing on the hump of Indra's bull. Puru inherits Madhyadesha (Pauravas).
Kuvalayasva slays the subterranean demon Dhundhu near modern Sambhar lake.
Mandhatri's empire spans 'from where the Sun rises to where it sets'. Epigraphically claimed by the Imperial Cholas.
Muchukunda aids the Devas, enters timeless yogic slumber, revered in Tamil Chola inscriptions and Tiruvarur temple traditions.

synchronisms.lunar_aila: Bharata (son of Dushyanta and Sakuntala, Gen 27/30)
synchronisms.notes: Bharata establishes the imperial name 'Bharata-varsha'. Contemporary Haihaya-Ayodhya rivalries.

synchronisms.yadava_branch: Haihaya wars; Jamadagni and Bhargava Rama (Parasurama)
synchronisms.notes: Harischandra renowned for absolute truth and Rajaswiya sacrifice.

synchronisms.solar_ayodhya: Sagara (slayer of Haihayas, Sakas, Yavanas, Kambojas, Paradas)
synchronisms.notes: Sagara performs Ashvamedha; his sons dig the ocean (Sagara). Sibi Chakravarti contemporary in northern/southern memory.

synchronisms.lunar_aila: Ajamidha (ancestor of Panchalas, Chedis, and Kurus)
synchronisms.notes: Descent of Ganga (Bhagirathi). Puranas and Tamil epigraphs venerate Bhagiratha.

synchronisms.solar_ayodhya: Rituparna (friend and instructor of Nala of Nishadha in Aksavidya)
synchronisms.notes: Synchronism between Ayodhya, Vidarbha (Damayanti), and Nishadha (Nala).

synchronisms.solar_ayodhya: Raghu (conqueror of Digvijaya, founder of Raghuvamsha)
synchronisms.notes: Raghu's Digvijaya establishes sovereignty across entire subcontinent.

synchronisms.lunar_aila: Kuru (eponymous founder of Kurukshetra and Kuruvamsha)
synchronisms.notes: Vasu's eldest son Brihadratha founds the Barhadratha dynasty of Magadha (Girivraja/Rajagriha).
Rama's exile, bridge to Lanka, defeat of Ravana. Southern dynasties (Cholas, Andhra Ikshvakus) anchor their direct lineages to Sri Rama.

synchronisms.magadha_branch: Jarasandha (son of Brihadratha, emperor of Magadha)
synchronisms.notes: Taksha founds Takshasila; Pushkara founds Pushkalavati (Gandhara). Jarasandha establishes Magadhan paramountcy.

synchronisms.solar_ayodhya: Brihadbala (allied with Kauravas, slain by Abhimanyu on Day 13)
synchronisms.lunar_aila: Pandavas (Yudhishthira, Bhima, Arjuna, Nakula, Sahadeva) & Abhimanyu
synchronisms.yadava_branch: Krishna guides Pandavas; Yadava fratricidal war and submersion of Dvaraka
synchronisms.magadha_branch: Sahadeva slain; son Somapi / Marjari succeeds at Rajagriha
synchronisms.notes: The Great Bharata War. Watershed turning point marking Kali Yuga transition (traditional Kali 3102 BCE; Pargiter chronological estimate c. 950 BCE).

magadha_imperial_succession.overview: The central imperial axis of India spanning over 1,500 years, moving from Rajagriha to Pataliputra.

dynasties.name: Barhadratha / Brihadratha Dynasty (Post-War line)
dynasties.founder: Somapi (son of Sahadeva, grandson of Jarasandha)
dynasties.terminal_king: Ripunjaya (slain by his minister Sunika / Pulika)
dynasties.historical_significance: Maintained the fortress capital of Girivraja (Rajgir) fortified with cyclopean stone walls.

dynasties.name: Pradyota Dynasty (Avanti and Magadha synchronism)
dynasties.significance: Synchronized with Gautama Buddha, Udayana of Kausambi, and Bimbisara.

dynasties.name: Haryanka & Shishunaga Dynasties
dynasties.duration: c. 544 BCE - 345 BCE (Epigraphical, Buddhist, and Puranic concordance)

prominent_rulers.achievements: Contemporary of Buddha and Mahavira; annexed Anga; fortified Rajagriha.
Subdued Vrijji confederacy; patronized First Buddhist Council at Rajagriha; built fort at Pataligrama.
Formally founded Pataliputra at the confluence of Ganga and Son.
Destroyed the power of Pradyotas of Avanti, uniting northern India.
Convened Second Buddhist Council at Vaishali; shifted capital permanently to Pataliputra.

dynasties.name: Nanda Dynasty (Nava Nandas)
dynasties.founder: Mahapadma Nanda (titled Sarva-Kshatrantaka - destroyer of all Kshatriyas, and Ekarat - sole sovereign)
dynasties.terminal_king: Dhana Nanda (Agrammes / Xandrames of Greek historians)
dynasties.significance: Built the first pan-Indian standing army (200,000 infantry, 80,000 cavalry, 6,000 war elephants) whose might deterred Alexander's forces at the Beas (Hyphasis).

rulers.achievements: Guided by Chanakya (Kautilya); overthrew Nandas; defeated Seleucus I Nicator; unified Bharata from Gandhara to Karnataka; retired to Shravanabelagola.
Maintained diplomatic ties with Antiochus I and Ptolemy II Philadelphus; consolidated Deccan conquests.
Conquered Kalinga; engraved Edicts across India in Brahmi and Kharosthi; dispatched Dharma missions to Sri Lanka, Syria, Egypt, Macedonia; patronized Third Buddhist Council.

rulers.king: Dasharatha, Samprati, Salisuka, Devavarman, Satadhanvan, Brihadratha
rulers.achievements: Last emperor Brihadratha assassinated by his Senapati Pushyamitra Shunga.

dynasties.name: Shunga, Kanva, and Andhra-Satavahana Successions
dynasties.details: Pushyamitra Shunga performs two Ashvamedhas (Patanjali's Mahabhashya, Ayodhya inscription of Dhanadeva); succeeded by Kanvas; power shifts to the Dakshinapatha under the Satavahana (Andhra-bhritya) dynasty (Simuka, Satakarni, Gautamiputra Satakarni, Vasishthiputra Pulumayi).

kosala_solar_line_brihadbala_to_sumitra.source: Vishnu Purana IV.22, Bhagavata Purana IX.12, Vayu Purana
kosala_solar_line_brihadbala_to_sumitra.puranic_anchor_verse: ऐक्ष्वाकाणामयं वंशः सुमित्रान्तो भविष्यति। यतस्तं प्राप्य राजानं संस्थां प्राप्स्यति वै कलौ॥ (Aikshvakanam ayam vamshah sumitranto bhavishyati | Yatas tam prapya rajanam samstham prapsyati vai kalau ||)

genealogy.name: Brihadbala
genealogy.event: Killed at Kurukshetra by Abhimanyu (Mahabharata Drona Parva).

genealogy.name: Prasenajit (Pasenadi of Kosala, historical contemporary of Buddha)
Sumitra
genealogy.event: Final monarch of the classical Kosala Ikshvaku line; extinguished during Mahapadma Nanda's expansions.

paurava_lunar_line_parikshit_to_kshemaka.source: Vishnu Purana IV.21, Bhagavata Purana IX.22, Matsya Purana 50
paurava_lunar_line_parikshit_to_kshemaka.puranic_anchor_verse: ब्रह्मक्षत्रस्य यो योनिर्वंशो देवर्षिसत्कृतः। क्षेमकं प्राप्य राजानं संस्थां प्राप्स्यति कलौ युगे॥ (Brahma-kshatrasya yo yonir vamsho devarshi-satkritah | Kshemakam prapya rajanam samstham prapsyati kalau yuge ||)

genealogy.name: Parikshit II
genealogy.event: Crowned by Yudhishthira at Hastinapura; protected by Krishna in Uttara's womb; listened to Srimad Bhagavatam from Sukadeva; ruled 60 years.

genealogy.name: Janamejaya III
genealogy.event: Performed Sarpa Satra at Takshasila; heard the Mahabharata recited by Vaisampayana.

genealogy.name: Satanika
genealogy.event: Studied the Vedas under Yajnavalkya and military science under Kripacharya.

genealogy.name: Adhisimakrishna
genealogy.event: Great 3-year sacrifice in Naimisharanya during his reign; Puranas recited by Suta Lomaharshana / Ugrasravas.

genealogy.name: Nichakshu
genealogy.event: When Hastinapura was washed away by the flooding Ganga, shifted capital to Kaushambi in Vatsa.

genealogy.name: Udayana
genealogy.event: Famous King of Vatsa (Kaushambi), hero of Bhasa's Svapnavasavadatta, contemporary of Buddha and Pradyota.

genealogy.name: Kshemaka
genealogy.event: Last descendant of the Pandava / Kuru imperial bloodline.

epigraphical_citations: Epigraphia Indica, Vol. XX (J.Ph. Vogel, 'Prakrit Inscriptions from Nagarjunikonda')
Epigraphia Indica, Vol. XXI (D.C. Sircar, 'More Inscriptions from Nagarjunikonda')
royal_titles_and_solar_claims: इक्ष्वाकु-कुल-कमल-विभात-दिवाकर (Ikshvaku-kula-kamala-vibhata-divakara - 'The radiant sun that causes the lotus of the Ikshvaku race to bloom')
इक्ष्वाकु-राज-प्रवर-ऋषि-वंश-प्रसूत (Ikshvaku-raja-pravara-rishi-vamsa-prasuta - 'Born in the exalted lineage of the royal sage Ikshvaku')
शत-सहस्र-हल-गो-शत-सहस्र-पदायि (Giver of hundreds of thousands of kine and ploughs of land)
अनेकाश्वमेध-वाजपेय-याजी (Performer of multiple Ashvamedha and Vajapeya sacrifices)

genealogy.significance: Founder of independent Vijayapuri sovereignty after the decline of the Satavahanas; staunch patron of Vedic dharma (Ashvamedha, Agnihotra, Agnishtoma) while his sisters, queens, and daughters actively endowed Mahachaityas for Buddhist monks.
Son of Chamtamula I; married princesses of the Saka Kshatrapas of Ujjain; golden age of Nagarjunakonda Buddhist and Shaivite art.
Reigned for at least 24 years; built the Pushpabhadrasvamin temple (Shaivite) and Sarvadeva temple, leaving classical Sanskrit prasastis.
Subdued by the rising Pallavas of Kanchi (Simhavarman / Sivaskandavarman).

deccan_epigraphical_bridge_andhra_ikshva.historiographical_analysis: The Andhra Ikshvakus prove that the Ikshvaku lineage of Kosala (Sri Rama's line) migrated southward across the Dandakaranya along the Krishna-Godavari river basin, maintaining unbroken memory of their descent from Manu and Ikshvaku, acting as the geographical and genealogical linchpin between northern Aryavarta and the far southern Tamil dynasties.

epigraphical_records.charter: Anbil Plates of Sundara Chola (Parantaka II, 10th century CE)
epigraphical_records.publication: Epigraphia Indica, Vol. XV, pp. 44-72 (Ed. T.A. Gopinatha Rao)
epigraphical_records.sanskrit_verses: Traces descent from Vishnu -> Brahma -> Marichi -> Kashyapa -> Vivasvan (Surya) -> Manu -> Ikshvaku -> Mandhata -> Muchukunda -> Sibi -> Chola (the eponymous king) -> Karikala -> Kocengannan -> Vijayalaya.

epigraphical_records.charter: Thiruvalangadu Plates of Rajendra Chola I (dated Regnal Year 6 = 1018 CE)
epigraphical_records.publication: South Indian Inscriptions, Vol. III, Part III, No. 205 (Ed. E. Hultzsch)
epigraphical_records.sanskrit_verses: Comprises 31 copper plates (largest found in India until Karandai). Sanskrit portion by poet Narayana: Surya -> Manu -> Ikshvaku -> Vikukshi -> Kakutstha (Puranjaya) -> Mandhatri -> Muchukunda -> Valabha -> Sibi (who gave his flesh to protect a dove) -> Chola -> Rajakesari -> Parakesari -> Mrityujit -> Vyaghraketu -> Karikala -> Kocengannan -> Vijayalaya -> Aditya I -> Parantaka I -> Rajaditya -> Gandaraditya -> Arinjaya -> Sundara Chola Parantaka II -> Rajaraja I -> Rajendra Chola I.

epigraphical_records.charter: Kanyakumari Stone Inscription of Virarajendra (11th century CE)
epigraphical_records.details: Exhaustive dynastic prashasti of 52 Sanskrit stanzas recording over fifty generations linking the solar sovereigns Mandhatri, Muchukunda, Sibi, and Kakutstha directly to Karikala and the Imperial Cholas.

sangam_literature_and_mythical_forebears.deed: Ringing of the Ara-Arazhi (Bell of Justice); condemned his own son to death under the wheels of the royal chariot to render equal justice to a grieving mother cow whose calf was crushed. The archetype of Dharma.

sangam_literature_and_mythical_forebears.textual_sources: Purananuru (verses 37, 39, 43, 46 by poets Tamappalkannanar, Kovur Kizhar), Manimekalai
sangam_literature_and_mythical_forebears.deed: Offered his own flesh cut from his body into the weighing scales to ransom the life of a dove sought by a hawk (Indra and Agni tested him). Chola kings took the proud title 'Sembiyan' (descendant of Sibi).

sangam_literature_and_mythical_forebears.tradition: Tiruvarur Thyagaraja Swami temple chronicle; Thiruvalangadu plates verse 14
sangam_literature_and_mythical_forebears.deed: Brought the seven Somaskanda lingas (Vitanka kshetras) given by Indra to Tiruvarur; defended the realm of Devas.

Won the Battle of Venni against combined Chera and Pandya forces; built the Kallanai (Grand Anicut) on the Kaveri river—one of the oldest water-diversion structures in the world; embarked on Himalayan expedition planting the Tiger crest on Mount Meru.

sangam_literature_and_mythical_forebears.textual_sources: Purananuru 74, Kalavali Narpathu (Poet Poygaiyar), Tirumangai Alvar's Periya Tirumozhi
sangam_literature_and_mythical_forebears.deed: Fought Chera king Kanaikkal Irumporai at Kalumalam; built 70 Mada-koyils (elevated temples inaccessible to elephants) dedicated to Lord Shiva, including Jambukeswaram (Thiruvanaikaval).

imperial_chola_historical_succession.event: Captured Thanjavur from Muttaraiyars; founded temple of Nisumbhasudani.
Defeated Pallava Aparajita at Sripurambiyam; crowned on the banks of Kaveri; built Shiva temples along the entire course of Kaveri.
Covered the Nataraja Sabha at Chidambaram with pure gold (Pon Veinda Perumal / Hemachhadita); issued Uttiramerur Inscriptions outlining democratic village sabha election system (Kudavolai).
Architect of the Brihadisvara Temple (Peruvudaiyar Koyil) at Thanjavur; subdued Pandya, Chera, Sinhala, Vengi realms; established naval supremacy across the Indian Ocean.
March to the Ganga defeating Mahipala of Bengal; brought holy water to build Gangaikondacholapuram and Cholagangam lake; trans-oceanic expedition conquering Srivijaya, Kadaram, Sumatra, and Malaya.

epigraphical_records.charter: Velvikkudi Copper Plates of Nedunjadaiyan (Parantaka Nedunjadaiyan, c. 770 CE)
epigraphical_records.publication: Epigraphia Indica, Vol. XVII, pp. 291-309 (Ed. H. Krishna Sastri)
epigraphical_records.sanskrit_and_tamil_content: Traces lineage from the Supreme Lord -> Brahma -> Atri -> Chandra (Soma) -> Budha -> Pururavas -> Pandyan lineage. Sage Agastya is identified as the perpetual preceptor (Kulaguru) of the dynasty. Records ancient ancestor Palyagashalai Mudukudumi Peruvaludhi granting the village Velvikkudi to Narkorran; revival after the dark Kalabhra interregnum by King Kadungon; succession down to Nedunjadaiyan.

epigraphical_records.charter: Larger Sinnamanur Plates of Rajasimha II (10th century CE)
epigraphical_records.publication: South Indian Inscriptions, Vol. III, Part IV, No. 206
epigraphical_records.epic_and_historical_content: Affirms descent from the Moon (Chandra). Mentions that the Pandya king shared the throne of Indra, broke the bracelets of Indra, weighed himself against Agastya, and immortalizes the foundation of the Tamil Sangam: 'Mahabharatam Tamil-paduthum Madhura-puri-sangam-vaiyyum' (establishing the Tamil Sangam in Madurai and having the Mahabharata translated into Tamil).

epigraphical_records.charter: Madras Museum Plates of Jatilavarman (c. 8th century CE)
epigraphical_records.details: Echoes the Velvikkudi prashasti, extolling the Pandyas as performers of Hiranyagarbha, Gosahasra, and Tulabhara sacrifices.

chandra_vamsha_lineage_and_agastya_tradi.lunar_descent: Brahma -> Atri -> Soma (Moon) -> Budha -> Pururavas -> Ayus -> Nahusha -> Yayati -> Pandya (eponymous southern scion).
chandra_vamsha_lineage_and_agastya_tradi.fish_emblem: The twin carp (Kayal) emblem of the Pandyas instituted by Pururavas, symbolizing cosmic oceanic dominion.
chandra_vamsha_lineage_and_agastya_tradi.agastya_the_kulaguru: According to the Velvikkudi plates and Tiruvilaiyadal Puranam, Agastya acted as the imperial chaplain, initiating the kings in statecraft and consecrating the capital at Madurai.
chandra_vamsha_lineage_and_agastya_tradi.the_three_sangams: According to Iraiyanar Ahaporul Commentary, the First Sangam (Mudhal Sangam) sat in Tenmadurai for 4,440 years under 89 kings from Kaysina Valudi to Kadungon; the Second Sangam (Idai Sangam) at Kapatapuram for 3,700 years; the Third Sangam (Kadai Sangam) at modern Madurai for 1,850 years under 49 kings down to Ukkiraperuvaludhi.

historical_early_medieval_pandya_kings.title: Destroyer of the Kalabhras; restorer of the Pandya kingdom and Vedic/Tamil traditions.
Victor at Nelveli; contemporary of Saivite Saint Tirugnanasambandar; embraced Saivism.
Defeated Ay chieftains and Western Gangas.
Defeated Pallavamalla Nandivarman at Sankaramangai; renovated Madurai walls.
Issuer of the Velvikkudi and Anaimalai grants; greatest early medieval Pandya warrior.

literary_and_epigraphical_sources: Padirruppattu (Ten Decads praising ten Chera monarchs)
Pugalur Brahmi Inscriptions (Arattanamalai, Karur, 2nd century CE)

traditions_and_genealogical_connections.concept: Perunchottu Uthiyan Cheralathan and the Bharata War
traditions_and_genealogical_connections.text: Purananuru v. 2: 'அலவும் மலர்ந்த வான்தலை தொடங்கி... ஐவரும் ஈரம்பதின்மரும் பொருத களத்து... பெருஞ்சோற்று மிகுபதம் வரையாது கொடுத்தோய்' (Alavum malarndha vana-thalai thodangi... Aivarum eerainbatthinmarum porudha kalatthu... Perum-chorru migupadam veruvadhu kodutha...)
traditions_and_genealogical_connections.meaning: When the Five (Pandavas) and the Hundred (Kauravas) fought on the battlefield of Kurukshetra, Cheralathan without limit provided nourishing feast (food) to both imperial armies. Demonstrates how Sangam kings anchored their political prestige to the pan-Indian Kurukshetra event.

traditions_and_genealogical_connections.concept: The Agastya - Velir Migration from Dvaraka
traditions_and_genealogical_connections.text: Nachinarkkiniyar (Tolkappiyam Payiram): Sage Agastya journeyed to Dvaraka, approached Lord Krishna (Vishnu), and led eighteen families of royal Velir chieftains (Patin-en-kudi Velir) and Arayar southward to establish agriculture, civilization, and settlements in the Tamil country.
traditions_and_genealogical_connections.meaning: Provides the direct historical-migration link connecting the Yadava/Vrishni clan of Dvaraka and Mathura to the ruling aristocracy of South India.

notable_kings.achievement: Marched to the Himalayas, carved the Bow emblem on the mountain rocks, and defeated northern kings on the Ganga.
Hero of Silappadikaram (Vanjikkandam); fetched stone from the Himalayas for the shrine of Kannagi (Pattini Devi); subdued Kanaka and Vijaya.

epigraphical_records.charter: Kuram Plates of Paramesvaravarman I (7th century CE)
epigraphical_records.publication: South Indian Inscriptions, Vol. I, No. 151
epigraphical_records.genealogy_recital: Traces descent from the Supreme Being -> Brahma -> Angiras -> Brihaspati -> Samyu -> Bharadvaja -> Drona -> Asvatthaman -> Pallava.

epigraphical_records.charter: Kasakudi Plates of Nandivarman II Pallavamalla (8th century CE)
epigraphical_records.publication: South Indian Inscriptions, Vol. II, Part III, No. 73
epigraphical_records.sanskrit_prasasti: Verses 1-10: Parabrahman -> Brahma -> Angiras -> Brihaspati -> Samyu -> Bharadvaja -> Drona (master of Dhanurveda) -> Asvatthaman (the immortal warrior-sage) -> Pallava (eponymous ancestor, born from an Apsaras / Naga princess) -> Asokavarman -> Kalabhartr -> Chutapallava -> Virakurcha -> Skandasishya -> Simhavarman -> Simhavishnu.

epigraphical_records.charter: Velurpalayam and Reyuru Plates (9th century CE)
epigraphical_records.details: Confirms the Brahma-Kshatriya status of the Pallavas of Kanchi, belonging to the Bharadvaja Gotra, combining Vedic ritual authority with unvanquished imperial arms.

historical_imperial_pallava_kings.event: Overthrew Kalabhras in Tondaimandalam; patronized Bharavi (author of Kiratarjuniya).
Pioneered rock-cut cave temples at Mandagapattu, Tiruchirappalli, Mamallapuram; wrote the Sanskrit farce Mattavilasa Prahasana; composed Kudumiyanmalai musical inscription.
Defeated Chalukya Pulakeshin II; captured and burnt Vatapi (Badami); carved the monolithic Rathas and Shore Temples of Mamallapuram; hosted Hiuen Tsang (Xuanzang) in 640 CE.
Built the magnificent Kailasanatha Temple at Kanchipuram and the Shore Temple at Mamallapuram; sent embassies to the Tang court of China.
Built the Vaikuntha Perumal Temple at Kanchipuram; patronized Vaishnava Saint Tirumangai Alvar; issuer of Kasakudi plates.

grand_synthesis_who_we_are.tamil_title: யார் நாம்? (Who We Are?): ஒருமைப்பட்ட பாரத நாகரிக மரபு

philosophical_and_historical_thesis.pillar: Cosmic Genesis and the Sacred Ontological Lineage
philosophical_and_historical_thesis.elaboration: From Brahma's contemplation down to the Saptarishis (Marichi, Atri, Angiras, Bharadvaja, Kashyapa, Agastya) and the Manus, Indian civilizational genealogy is not an accidental biological catalogue, but a sacred transmission of Cosmic Order (Rta) and Righteousness (Dharma). Every historical ruler conceived their royal duty as the earthly maintenance of cosmic harmony.

philosophical_and_historical_thesis.pillar: The Inseparable Unity of Solar and Lunar Currents (Surya & Chandra Vamsha)
philosophical_and_historical_thesis.elaboration: The subcontinent was never partitioned into alien racial domains. The Solar line (Ikshvaku, Kakutstha, Mandhatri, Sibi, Sri Rama) governed Ayodhya, flourished in the Deccan with the Andhra Ikshvakus, and achieved imperial zenith with the Cholas in Tamilakam. The Lunar line (Pururavas, Bharata, Kuru, Yadu, Sri Krishna, Parikshit) governed Hastinapura, Kaushambi, Dvaraka, and Mathura, while simultaneously guiding the Pandyan emperors of Madurai and the Chera kings across the Western Ghats.

The Pallavas of Kanchipuram, claiming descent through Bharadvaja, Drona, and Ashvatthaman, embodied the indivisibility of wisdom and strength. The sword of the king was sanctified by the mantra of the Rishi. Similarly, Agastya stood as the spiritual architect who connected the northern Himalayan hermitage to the southern Podhigai hills, authoring Tamil grammar and consecrating Pandyan crowns.

philosophical_and_historical_thesis.pillar: Sacred Geography and Daily Sankalpa Memory
philosophical_and_historical_thesis.elaboration: For millennia, every individual performing an ablution, Vedic ritual, or temple archana throughout the subcontinent chants the identical geographical coordinate: 'Jambudvipe Bharata-varshe Bharata-khande Dandakaranye / Mero-dakshina-parsve...'. This living liturgical memory matches perfectly with the epigraphical reality of copper plates from Kashmir to Kanyakumari.

Nineteenth-century European race-theories attempted to manufacture an artificial schism between 'Aryan' and 'Dravidian', North and South, Sanskrit and Tamil. The physical copper plates of the Cholas, Pandyas, Pallavas, and Cheras provide incontrovertible, self-authored proof that the ancient Tamil kings saw themselves as the purest heirs to Manu, Ikshvaku, Sibi, Pururavas, and Bharadvaja. Sanskrit and Tamil flourished as the twin eyes of the single civilizational soul.

philosophical_and_historical_thesis.pillar: The Eternal Answer: யார் நாம்? (Who We Are?)
philosophical_and_historical_thesis.elaboration: We are the inheritors of an unbroken civilizational continuum spanning from the primordial rishis and epic emperors down to the village assemblies of Uttiramerur and the grand gopurams of Thanjavur and Madurai. We are the sons and daughters of Bharata Varsha—a civilization where sacred memory, epigraphical stone, and living practice remain one.
